scenes.title: 허수는 왜 등장할까?
lines: To understand this approach to rotation through multiplication, we first extend the number system. The square of a real number is nonnegative, so no real number squares to minus one.
We define a new rule in which i squared is minus one. The number i defined this way is called the imaginary unit.
This rule does not make an imaginary number a hidden object inside the game. It provides a useful numerical tool for direction calculations.
To see why it helps with rotation, we will represent these numbers as point coordinates.

scenes.title: 아이를 곱하면 왜 90도 돌아갈까?
lines: A complex number a+bi represents a point (a,b) in a plane. Its horizontal coordinate is the real part and its vertical coordinate is the coefficient of i.
The point with x coordinate two and y coordinate one is 2+i. Multiplying by i gives 2i+i squared, which equals minus one plus 2i.
The new x coordinate is minus one and the new y coordinate is two. The arrow turns ninety degrees counterclockwise while retaining length square root of five.
Multiplying a point (a,b) by i changes it to (-b,a), allowing multiplication to represent a planar turn.
In three dimensions, we also need an axis that defines the rotation plane. We will extend this direction calculation to a quaternion using that axis.

scenes.title: 정규화는 방향을 고치는 일이 아니다
lines: Normalization means changing the norm to one. For [3,0,0,4], the norm is the square root of three squared plus four squared, which is five.
Divide all four components by five. The scalar becomes 0.6, both x and y remain zero, and z becomes 0.8. The squared norm is 0.36 plus 0.64, which equals one.
The numerical magnitude changes while the axis and component ratios remain. This does not correct a wrongly selected axis or multiplication order.
Likewise, faster character motion does not require a larger orientation quaternion norm. We will observe speed and orientation separately in the game.

scenes.title: 같은 벡터로 한쪽 곱과 양쪽 곱을 비교
lines: The initial complex example used one multiplication in a plane. To verify the earlier half-angle explanation, we return to the ninety-degree z-axis example. The input vector has x component one, y zero and z one.
To put a vector into the quaternion expression, prepend scalar zero. Define the letter C as square root of two divided by two. The rotation has scalar C, x and y zero, and z C.
The left multiplication alone produces scalar minus C and three vector components equal to C. Its nonzero scalar shows that this is not yet a three-dimensional direction vector.
Also multiply by the inverse on the right. That inverse has scalar C, x and y zero, and z minus C. The complete result has scalar zero, x zero, y one and z one.

Removing scalar zero leaves vector (0,1,1). The z component parallel to the rotation axis remains one while the original x component turns into y. The complete two-sided calculation verifies what the half-angle operation does.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 05
lines: We have defined a 90-degree turn about z. Returning to the game, we can watch body directions change together; the angle projected by a moving camera is not our defined world angle.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 06
lines: We saw the whole orientation change. What happens if we apply the same 90-degree turn again? We will calculate a fixed-axis example rather than measure a particular game maneuver.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 08
lines: Different component signs represented the same final orientation. Can that orientation reveal the preceding motion? Let us follow one interval through time.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 12
lines: Orientation and speed were separate quantities. Let us now undo a stored rotation; the unit-length condition we maintained makes this calculation simpler.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 17
lines: The order of fixed-axis rotations changed the result. In the game, watch how turning the body also changes its attached directions; this motivates separating world and body frames.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 23
lines: Our calculation turned x toward y while preserving the component parallel to the axis. We will now observe body directions separately from the camera frame that projects them on screen.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 26
lines: We completed a rotation and its inverse. Using that result, let us return to our opening question: what do the four numbers store, and which operations do they support?

scenes.title: 두 편의 지도와 첫 편의 질문
lines: This quaternion lecture has two episodes. After outlining the complete journey, this first episode explains how to construct a stored rotation and undo it.

scenes.title: 구십 도에서 다른 각도로 넓히기
lines: We verified that multiplying by i produces a ninety-degree turn. How can we represent other angles?
Recall the unit circle from high-school trigonometry. A unit arrow turned by theta has horizontal component cos(theta) and vertical component sin(theta).
Multiplication by cos(theta)+i sin(theta) therefore rotates the plane by theta. At ninety degrees the cosine is zero and the sine is one, giving i.
This planar calculation uses the full physical angle theta. When the three-dimensional quaternion later uses a half-angle, we will compare the different operation applied to the vector.

scenes.title: 첫 편의 결과가 다음 편의 질문으로
lines: We have connected the four components to a computational representation of axis and angle, rather than four spatial directions.
Starting from a complex planar turn, we constructed a quaternion with a unit axis and half-angle, checked its norm, and verified that an inverse cancels the applied operation.
A game orientation rarely stops after one turn. The next episode explains why the order of two turns matters and calculates the extra rotation from a current orientation to a target.

scenes.title: 두 번째 편의 질문과 앞 편의 결과
lines: The first episode constructed a rotation and used its inverse to undo an operation. This episode composes turns and calculates how to reach a target direction.

After observing a bicycle's orientation, we reverse the order of the same two turns and compare their results. We then find the rotation from a current orientation to a target and verify it on an actual direction vector.
We begin with a counteracting tilt, distinguishing an orientation reversal from reversing the traveled path.

scenes.title: 숫자 세 개가 담는 방향을 날개로 관찰하기
lines: Let us connect the three axis components to a visible orientation. This bicycle-to-flight excerpt has broad wings that make a tilt easier to read.
Follow the red line between the two visible wing tips. The teal line is a screen-horizontal reference. Their changing relationship shows a projected tilt.
The camera also moves, so this is not a measured world rotation. We now choose a camera-independent axis and construct four components from that axis and an angle.

scenes.title: 속도 숫자와 자세값의 길이를 나누기
lines: The normalized quaternion has norm one. Compare the speed display on the right with a direction line attached to the visible character.
Changing from bicycle travel to flight substantially changes the displayed speed. A red wing line shows orientation, while the character and route show changing position.
The same orientation can move faster, and similar speeds can accompany different tilts. A larger speed number does not imply a larger orientation quaternion norm.
Near the end, flight equipment changes back to a bicycle. Camera distance and apparent object size also change, while our defined unit-rotation condition remains the same.
We have not measured this game's internal values. We are separating the verified mathematical condition from visible speed, position and orientation. Keep that separation in the following example.

scenes.title: 역회전은 주행 경로의 되감기가 아니다
lines: We verified that the conjugate of a unit rotation is its inverse. Track the red torso line separately from the bicycle's position as it banks and corrects its direction.
Even when the tilt becomes smaller, the bicycle continues forward. Orientation and position changes have different inputs and outputs.
Multiplying by an inverse cancels the defined rotation. It does not cancel elapsed time, collisions or traveled distance.
Our previous value had norm one. Would the conjugate alone also invert a component tuple with norm two? The next calculation checks that condition.

scenes.title: 변화가 없다는 연산도 입력과 결과로 읽기
lines: An ending orientation cannot recover every preceding action. Snow travel makes it easier to separate the traveled route from directions attached to the body.
A red line follows the torso and a blue line follows the visible skis. Observe how both change on bends and sloping terrain.
Identity rotation does not mean that speed, position and camera motion all stop. It is an operation that returns the input direction unchanged.
Treat one body direction as the input. Applying no extra rotation should return that same direction as the result.
Which four components guarantee this result? The next diagram removes the moving background and verifies the same input and output.

scenes.title: 같은 끝 자세와 지나온 회전 과정을 구분하기
lines: The equality of orientations represented by q and minus q concerns the ending state. Follow a moving jump and landing to see the limits of that statement.
The rider follows a slope, changes posture in the air and returns to the snow. Follow the red torso line and the blue ski line in that order.
Recovering the intermediate directions requires watching the motion or retaining a time record. One ending orientation does not contain the entire process.
Similar ending directions do not establish identical actions. Conversely, opposite signs of a stored quaternion do not establish opposite orientations.
A following camera also changes the projected reference. These lines support observation; they do not measure accumulated world rotation.
We have separated component signs, visible ending orientation and motion through time. The following example checks which information an orientation value can store.

scenes.title: 평면의 회전에서 삼차원 축으로
lines: A planar turn used one angle. An airborne bicycle also needs a selected rotation axis.
Follow the visible body direction to see why a three-dimensional axis is added.

scenes.title: 반각은 화면에서 절반만 도는 뜻이 아니다
lines: We constructed a stored rotation from an axis and half-angle. Follow the bicycle's torso and wheel directions together; our goal is to represent the complete orientation change.
Half-angle does not mean that the visible object turns only halfway to the target. It enters the stored-value formula, and vector application uses the complete two-sided multiplication.
Keep that distinction while observing the body-attached directions in the following excerpt.

scenes.title: 기울기를 상쇄할 때 남는 이동
lines: We separated speed from orientation. Compare separate bicycle and flight excerpts here. The backtracking interface is excluded, and these cuts are not presented as one continuous action.
During flight the red wing line changes while speed and position keep changing. A value that cancels an orientation operation does not reverse the entire motion.
How do we construct the value that undoes rotation itself? Using the verified unit-norm condition, we next calculate a conjugate by reversing the vector-part signs.

scenes.title: 한 번의 변화에서 두 번의 연산으로
lines: Body-attached directions move with the object. Follow the red torso line and blue wheel line as the bicycle passes slopes and jumps.
We now return to calculation and apply our defined ninety-degree turn about the same axis twice. Rather than infer game internals, we directly compare the input, first result and second result.

scenes.title: 고정 축과 몸체 축을 분리해 관찰하기
lines: Reversing the same two defined turns changed the result. Separate a red body-attached direction from a teal screen reference during this ride.
The body direction changes with the tilt. We must specify whether the next operation uses that body frame or a fixed world frame.
The teal screen line is not a measured world axis. It distinguishes the moving camera observation from the fixed-axis calculation in the diagram.
Having observed a moving body reference, follow intermediate action order in the next snowboard and bicycle excerpts.

scenes.title: 현재 자세에서 목표 자세를 묻기
lines: We distinguished action order and reference frames. Observe the bicycle following a bend while considering its current orientation and a separately chosen target orientation.
The changing red torso line describes orientation; advancing along the route describes position. Landing location and landing direction are different targets.
The image does not supply exact target quaternion data. The next calculation defines current orientation a and target b, then asks which extra rotation produces b.

scenes.title: 최소 자세 차이와 동작 전체의 길이
lines: The minimum angle from the quaternion dot product measures the difference between two ending orientations. Observe successive jumps and bends to see the scope of that value.
Follow the red torso line and blue wheel line. Orientation changes in the jump, and travel continues after landing.
Selecting different current and target instants changes the two orientations being compared. Distance to a target position is a separate quantity.
We omitted an interval where another player occludes the body. The two excerpts are not asserted to be the before and after of one jump; compare the visible motion within each cut.
A minimum orientation difference does not reconstruct the order or total amount of preceding rotation. A trick history and an ending orientation need different records.
After further observing target orientation in the following excerpt, we will calculate which quantity changes when applying only part of a selected rotation.

scenes.title: 절반 회전은 네 숫자의 절반이 아니다
lines: With a target orientation chosen, consider applying only part of the turn. First observe the bicycle changing posture during a jump and continuing along the route.
Following the red torso and blue wheel lines separates orientation changes from the continuing position changes.
We have not measured an exact half-angle turn in this footage. Our next defined calculation asks how to obtain forty-five degrees from a ninety-degree rotation.
Halving all four components first breaks the unit-norm condition. The earlier normalization example separates numerical magnitude from physical rotation angle.
We retain the axis and apply a multiplier to the angle. We will introduce logarithm and exponential notation by explaining what they record and reconstruct.

scenes.title: 계산한 벡터를 물체에 붙여 읽기
lines: We verified a rotated vector. Read different bicycle directions together, such as the red torso line and blue wheel line.
Distinguish the moving-camera image from world-orientation calculation as we continue into the next excerpt.

scenes.title: 반대 기울기에서 두 회전의 합성으로
lines: An inverse cancels an applied rotation. In this separate riding excerpt, follow the red torso direction and blue visible wheel contour together.
A bend changes both the tilt and the facing direction. To compose our two defined rotations into one orientation, can we simply add the four components?

The upcoming calculation uses a dot product to compare directions and a cross product to produce a perpendicular vector. We first verify these tools with small numbers, then read the Hamilton product.
